name: Wei Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Wei, thanks for joining me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a crew putting up mass timber buildings, big engineered wood panels and beams, mostly four- and five-storey offices and a care home at the moment. A crane lifts the panels in and we guide them, fix the brackets, and screw everything together. I'm also the one who runs the layout robot, a little machine that drives around the concrete slab and prints the wall lines on the floor from the drawings. I love when a floor goes up in a day. What I don't love is the waiting, when the crane's stopped for wind and twenty of us are just standing there.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Hanna does the books part time for the farm supply store. We've got Lars, he's twelve, and Mei, she's nine. Church on Sundays, and I coach Lars's football team. On weekends I build decks and pergolas with my brother-in-law Erik, cash in hand on the side, nothing big. We've got around four months saved. I use AI tools every day, for quoting the decks, checking drawings, even planning the football drills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still a great tool, people just expected too much. I'd keep telling the guys on site it saves time on the boring bits. I'd post a few videos of the layout robot, because people love watching it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing much changes, and that's fine. I've got an edge with the tools, and I'd keep using it to win more deck jobs on weekends. I'd be a bit let down, I'll admit, because I enjoy the new stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep the side business going. Maybe Erik and I would buy a second-hand mini digger for the footings, so we can take bigger garden jobs. We'd keep putting a bit away each month like normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored, maybe. Like a film that ends before the big scene.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the layout robot. How did you end up running it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody else wanted to. The site manager unboxed it, read the manual for five minutes and said, Wei, you're good with phones. I spent two evenings learning it, and now it saves us a day of chalk lines per floor. My foreman still calls it my pet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the side business like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small. Maybe two jobs a month in summer, one in spring and autumn. I use the AI to draw the deck in 3D for the customer and work out the timber order to the nearest board. Erik does the talking, I do the numbers. It pays for holidays and the kids' sports.

S0.say: It's still a great tool, people just expected too much. I'd keep telling the guys it saves time on the boring bits and post videos of the layout robot.
S0.think: Nothing much changes for me, and that's fine, because my edge with the tools helps me win weekend deck jobs. I'd be a bit let down, since I enjoy the new stuff.
S0.do: Keeps working and running the weekend deck business with his brother-in-law. Considers buying a second-hand mini digger for bigger garden jobs and saves as usual.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit bored, like a film ending before the big scene.
S0.quote: My foreman still calls it my pet.
S0.fieldNote: Wei is the crew's go-to for new technology and already runs a small side business. He'd be mildly disappointed by a plateau but secure. He sees tools as a way to grow his own income. Family, church and coaching his son's team anchor his week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like any big change: the people who learn it early do well, and the ones who wait get squeezed. I'd tell the young guys on site to get stuck in. I don't think the government should be propping up jobs that don't make sense anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well out of this. More robots on site means someone has to run them, and I already do. And with the side business, I could use the same tools to do jobs with fewer people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the firm to send me on every course for new site robots and drones. I'd spend some savings, maybe 2,000, on better gear for the deck business, a good laser level and design software. I'd try to grow the side work to three or four jobs a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even excited. It feels like the kind of change I'm built for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of the older guys. There's a carpenter, Frank, 58, best I've seen with a chisel, but he won't touch a phone. I'd try to help him, but I can't make him learn. Some people would rather go down with the ship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government shouldn't prop up jobs. What if it were Frank's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's hard when it's someone you know. I'd still say the answer is apprenticeships and the church and families helping, not handouts. But I'd personally try to find him something, maybe on the deck jobs, where his hands still matter.

S1.say: The people who learn it early do well, and the ones who wait get squeezed. I'd tell the young guys to get stuck in, and I don't think the government should prop up jobs that no longer make sense.
S1.think: I think I'd do well out of this, because more site robots means someone has to run them and I already do. I could use the same tools to run my side jobs with fewer people.
S1.do: Asks the firm for every course on new site robots and drones, and spends about 2,000 of savings on a laser level and design software for the deck business. Aims to grow the side work to three or four jobs a month.
S1.feel: Calm and even excited, feeling built for this kind of change.
S1.quote: There's a carpenter, Frank, 58, best I've seen with a chisel, but he won't touch a phone.
S1.fieldNote: Wei sees steady disruption as an opportunity and plans to invest his own money. His free-market views are softened when he thinks about a specific older colleague, and he'd try to help him personally. He believes in family and church support over state help. He is confident and energetic here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, okay, this is huge, and everyone needs to move fast. I'd still say it's better for people to adapt and build things than to wait for government cheques. But I'd admit it's hitting faster than anyone can keep up with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one worries me. If AI can do almost anything in two years, then running the layout robot isn't a job anymore, the robot runs itself. My edge is gone. And the deck business, someone with a robot and a van could undercut us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. I'd use savings to get a robot or two for the deck business as soon as they're on the market, probably leased, so Erik and I are the ones undercutting others, not being undercut. I'd keep the day job as long as it lasts and put every extra bit into savings. I'd try to line up a few long-term maintenance contracts with the care home and offices we built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be pushing hard, but I'd feel the ground moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Hanna?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're going to be careful but not scared. She's the sensible one with money. She'd want to know exactly what the robot lease would cost and how many jobs to pay it off. Then she'd probably say yes, because she knows I'll work for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't spending savings on robots risky when the whole market is changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd only lease, not buy, and only with a couple of jobs already booked. If it went wrong, we'd have a few months saved and family nearby. It's a risk, but sitting still is a bigger one.

S2.say: This is huge and everyone needs to move fast. I'd still say it's better to adapt and build things than to wait for government cheques, but it's hitting faster than anyone can keep up with.
S2.think: This one worries me, because running the layout robot isn't a job if the robot runs itself. My edge is gone, and someone with a robot and a van could undercut our deck business.
S2.do: Leases a robot or two for the deck business as soon as they're available, only with jobs already booked, so he and his brother-in-law can undercut others. Keeps the day job while it lasts, saves every extra bit and lines up maintenance contracts with buildings his crew put up.
S2.feel: Anxious, pushing hard while feeling the ground move.
S2.quote: My edge is gone. And the deck business, someone with a robot and a van could undercut us.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture is the first that shakes Wei, because it wipes out both his tech advantage and his side business edge. He responds by taking a calculated risk on robots rather than pulling back. His free-market stance holds, though he admits the pace is beyond anyone. He relies on his wife's financial caution as a check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for people to get ready if they stop moaning and start learning. Find what you can own or run, and do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a good window for me. I could grow the side business into a proper company with robots, while still getting a wage for a couple of years. I'd be 48 and owning something, instead of working for someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd register the deck business properly, get insurance and an accountant, Hanna would probably do the books. I'd lease our first robot in year two, once the reviews are in, and take on bigger jobs, garden rooms and small extensions. I'd keep building up savings, maybe an extra 200 a month while I still have the wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, because the end point is still big. But mostly I'd feel like I've got a head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you hire people, or just robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, if I could. I'd want to take on a young apprentice, maybe from church, and teach them to run the machines and deal with customers. That's how it should work, you bring people up with you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the end point's still big. What happens to your company in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. If AI can run the whole thing, maybe the big companies take over everything. I'd hope people still want a local guy they know from church and football. That's my bet, but it's a bet.

S3.say: Five years is enough for people to get ready if they stop moaning and start learning. Find something you can own or run, and do it.
S3.think: Five years is a good window for me to grow the side business into a proper company with robots while I still earn a wage. I'd be 48 and owning something instead of working for someone.
S3.do: Registers the deck business properly in the first year with insurance and an accountant, with his wife doing the books. Leases a first robot in year two once reviews are in, takes on garden rooms and small extensions, and saves an extra 200 a month while still earning a wage.
S3.feel: Uneasy because the end point is still big, but mostly feeling he has a head start.
S3.quote: I'd hope people still want a local guy they know from church and football. That's my bet, but it's a bet.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Wei plan to become an owner rather than an employee. He wants to bring on an apprentice from his church, true to his belief in work and community. He's honest that local trust is a bet, not a certainty. The extra time turns anxiety into a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift. Anyone who's willing to learn has time to set themselves up. The government's job is to make it easy to start a business and train apprentices, then get out of the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'd be 53, with the kids grown. I could build a proper business over that time, robots and all, and maybe step back from the heavy work. I think I'd come out of it okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the deck business steadily over five years, buy robots once they're cheap and proven, and maybe leave the day job around year five. I'd want Lars and Mei to learn both the tools and the people side. I'd keep saving and paying down the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Ten years feels like enough time to get ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lars about his future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's twelve, he'll be 22 by then. I'd tell him learn how things are built, learn how the machines think, and learn how to talk to people. Whatever happens, the guy who can do all three will find something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the slow version that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe that people get lazy. With ten years, a lot of guys on my crew would say, it's ages away. Then year nine comes and they're shocked. I'd try to get Frank and the others moving, but you can't push grown men.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift, and anyone willing to learn has time to set themselves up. The government's job is to make it easy to start a business and train apprentices, then get out of the way.
S4.think: At 53, with the kids grown, I could have built a proper business with robots and stepped back from the heavy work. I think I'd come out of it okay.
S4.do: Grows the deck business steadily over five years, buys robots once they're cheap and proven, and may leave the day job around year five. Keeps saving, pays down the mortgage and encourages his children to learn both the tools and the people side.
S4.feel: Calm, because ten years feels like enough time to get ahead of it.
S4.quote: Then year nine comes and they're shocked.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Wei is calm and confident in his plan to own a robot-assisted business. His worry shifts to colleagues who will put off acting. His advice to his son blends building, technology and people skills. His free-market and family values stay consistent throughout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Even if you're quick, two years isn't enough to build anything solid. What would help is making it easy and cheap to start a small business and lease the machines, and apprenticeships so young people learn the new trades instead of sitting at home.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether people like me want the robots. I do. I'm tired of carrying beams. I just want to be the one who owns the robot, not the one it replaces.

headlineQuote: I just want to be the one who owns the robot, not the one it replaces.
portrait: Wei is a 43-year-old carpenter on a mass timber crew who also runs the site's layout robot, with a wife who keeps books part time, two children, about four months of savings and a weekend deck business with his brother-in-law. He uses AI every day and sees new technology as a chance to own something. He stays calm in the mild pictures and plans to invest in tools and his side business. The fast AGI picture makes him anxious because his edge disappears, but he answers by leasing robots rather than retreating. With more time he plans to grow a robot-assisted business, and his free-market, family and church values stay steady throughout.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because even someone quick can't build anything solid in two years.
whatWouldHelp: Making it easy and cheap to start a small business and lease machines, and apprenticeships so young people learn the new trades.
